pages.name: Fifty readings
pages.text: Fifty readings have piled up round 27.00 V. A pile hides the order the readings came in. Tipped onto its side, the readings peel off in the order taken. The mean so far writes itself beside them. [[Noise]] is the random scatter every reading has. One reading on its own tells you little, because noise moves every reading. What matters is the trend over many.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings of a battery bank's float voltage pour from a hopper over 27.00 volts through a field of pegs and pile up on a beam balanced at their mean. The pile has tipped onto its side against the right edge, and the readings lie in the order taken along a thread, with the mean so far beside them.

pages.name: Two orders
pages.task: The same fifty readings come in two different orders. In one they creep up steadily. In the other they jumble. What tells the two apart?
pages.answer: Plotting them in the order taken
pages.why: The pile, its mean and its SD use only the values, so they come out the same for both orders. Laid out in the order taken, one order climbs and the other jumbles. Here the beads re-sort into the creeping order, and the pile on its side stays just the same.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings laid out in the order taken, jumbled, with the pile on its side at the right. The same fifty readings re-sort into a creeping order that climbs from left to right. The pile on its side stays exactly the same.
options: Plotting them in the order taken

pages.name: The best-fit line
pages.text: A flat line at the mean tilts into the [[best-fit line]]. That is the straight line that sits closest to all fifty. A [[drift]] is a steady change, so the readings climb along a slope. The line's slope measures the drift per reading. The trend tile gives it per 10 readings. The line always passes through the mean point. That point sits at the mean reading number and the mean voltage. Here the drift is 0.008 V per 10 readings, and the readings climb along the line.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings in the order taken, with the best-fit line through them, the line the rule would give without noise, and the mean point.

pages.name: How far it climbs
pages.task: The trend tile reads +0.008 V per 10 readings. About how far does the line climb from the first reading to the fiftieth?
pages.why: From the first reading to the fiftieth is 49 steps, about five lots of 10. So the line climbs about 0.008 × 4.9, which is about 0.04 V. The bracket at the end of the line now marks that climb.

pages.name: Noise leans it too
pages.text: Here the drift is zero, and a fresh batch has dropped. The line still leans a little, a different way each time. Each batch's random errors happen to sit a little higher at one end. The line follows them, because it fits whatever readings it gets. That lean is noise. In this simulation, with no drift, 95 batches in 100 lean by less than about 0.006 V per 10 readings either way. A drift bigger than that noise leans the line the same way, batch after batch.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings with no drift, in the order taken, with their best-fit line and the flat line the rule would give without noise.

pages.name: A lean of +0.003
pages.task: A fresh batch's trend tile reads +0.003 V per 10 readings. Noise alone leans the line by under about 0.006 V per 10 readings in 95 batches in 100. What does that show?
pages.answer: Nothing on its own, as noise alone leans the line that much now and then
pages.why: +0.003 is well inside the 0.006 that noise alone gives, so it shows nothing on its own. In fact no drift is set here, so all of the lean is noise. The lines of eight more batches now fan in, leaning either way.
pages.alt: A fresh batch of fifty simulated readings, with a best-fit line that leans a little up. The best-fit lines of eight more batches with no drift fan in. Some lean up and some lean down.
options: Nothing on its own, as noise alone leans the line that much now and then
The voltage drifts up 0.003 V per 10 readings

pages.name: Runs
pages.text: The run tile counts the most readings in a row each higher than the last, or each lower. With pure noise, six readings come in 720 orders, all equally likely. One climbs and one falls, so a given six run one way about 1 time in 360. Fifty noisy readings usually give a longest run of 3 to 5. A run needs a change per reading as big as the noise, as in the insulation tests ahead. Even the largest drift is far smaller, so it shows only in the fitted line.
pages.alt: Fifty simulated readings in the order taken, with the longest run of readings each higher than the last, or each lower, picked out.

pages.name: Four in a row
pages.task: Pure noise, four readings in a row. What is the chance they climb all the way?
pages.why: Four different readings can come in 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 orders. With pure noise, each order is equally likely. Only one climbs all the way, so the chance is 1 in 24. The steps are not separate coin tosses, because each shares a reading with the next.
pages.alt: Four simulated readings in a row, joined by a thread, in one jumbled order. All 24 orders of four readings are laid out in a grid. Only the first climbs all the way, and only the last falls all the way.
options: 1 in 8, as each step up is a coin toss

pages.name: Insulation resistance
pages.text: Now the beads are sixteen insulation resistance tests on a pump motor's winding, one a quarter. They sit on a scale by factors. As measured, they zigzag. Some test days were warmer, and warm insulation reads low. Corrected to 20 °C, as here, a steady fall shows. The longest run down often reaches six or more. This string was picked to show one. Read the line only across the tests you have. Past the last one, it is a guess.

pages.name: Correct to 20 °C
pages.task: A winding tested at 30 °C reads 300 MΩ. Using the rule of thumb, what does it read corrected to 20 °C?
pages.why: The rule of thumb halves the resistance for every 10 °C warmer. At 20 °C the winding is 10 °C cooler, so it reads double: 300 × 2 = 600 MΩ. Here each test taken at 30 °C now hops up by a factor of 2 to its corrected place.

pages.name: Same cause
pages.text: Two strings run over the same days: a pump bearing's temperature and a battery's float current. The air swings ±3 °C each day, and the rule makes both follow it. Over time they rise and fall together. Folded, as here, each pair is one point, the current against the bearing. The points line up closely, near 0.9 on the tile. How closely they line up is their [[correlation]]. Yet neither drives the other. The air drives both. With the air steady, they make a round cloud.
pages.alt: Two strings of simulated readings over the same days: a pump bearing's temperature above and a battery's float current below, with the air temperature between them. Folded, each pair becomes one point, current against bearing, lining up along a best-fit line.

pages.name: Show a cause
pages.task: A winding's insulation resistance and its temperature line up closely in your records. How could you show that warmth lowers the resistance?
pages.answer: Test one winding at two temperatures, with everything else kept the same
pages.why: A close line-up alone cannot say which drives which, or whether something else drives both. So change one thing yourself and keep the rest the same. Here the winding's last test is repeated the same day, 10 °C warmer. It reads half as much, and nothing else changed.

pages.name: Six falling
pages.task: Corrected to 20 °C, a motor's last six tests each read lower than the one before. Every reading is still above the example minimum. What do you make of it?
pages.answer: A steady fall, rare by chance, so look into it now
pages.why: From noise alone, a given six run one way about 1 time in 360. So six falling in a row is very likely a real fall, not noise, even while every reading passes. Look into it now. Read the line only across the tests you have. Here the last tests ring one after another as they fall.
